stemMd: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?
instructionsMd: Answer on the basis of the passage only.

options.label: A
options.textMd: The maxim that ignorance of the law excuses no one was unjust to citizens from its very origins.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Medieval heralds informed citizens of new laws more reliably than printed notices were later able to.

options.label: C
options.textMd: A change in how laws were made known quietly moved the burden of knowing them onto the governed.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Printed edicts improved the way law was communicated by fixing its wording and multiplying its copies.

explanationMd:
A central-claim question asks for the idea the whole passage is built to establish, so look at where the argument ends up and check that every paragraph feeds it.

The passage moves in four steps. Under proclamation, the authority had to tell each quarter of the city (paragraph one), which is why the maxim about ignorance was then "very nearly true" (paragraph two). Posting changed this: the law "no longer came to find the citizen" (paragraph three). The conclusion draws the consequence: "The burden of knowing the law had passed, almost without comment, from those who made it to those who had to obey it" (paragraph four).

So the central claim is that a change in the way laws were made known shifted, without anyone announcing it, the burden of knowing them onto the people governed.

**How to check.** A good statement of the main point should be one that every paragraph supports. The medieval description sets up the "before", the account of posting supplies the "after", and the final paragraph names the shift. The other choices each fit at most one paragraph, or contradict one.

distractorRationale.d: This is the "story of improvement" that the third paragraph says is usually told. The author grants that it is true but immediately adds that "something else changed as well"; the passage exists to point to that something else, so this is a conceded background view, not the central claim.
distractorRationale.b: The passage never compares how reliable heralds and printed notices were. It even lists dependence on a herald's voice and memory as a drawback that printing removed. Its contrast is about who had to go and find whom, not about accuracy.
distractorRationale.a: This contradicts the second paragraph, which says the maxim "sat comfortably" with the medieval arrangement and was then "very nearly true". The passage argues that the maxim's meaning changed later, not that it was unjust from the start.

accessibilityText: A question about the accompanying passage on the proclamation of laws. It asks which statement best expresses the central claim of the passage. The four answer options are: the maxim that ignorance of the law excuses no one was unjust to citizens from its very origins; medieval heralds informed citizens of new laws more reliably than printed notices were later able to; a change in how laws were made known quietly moved the burden of knowing them onto the governed; printed edicts improved the way law was communicated by fixing its wording and multiplying its copies.
